newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Testing times ahead for South African economy.
newsitem.headline: Testing times ahead for South African economy.

text.p: South Africa's new democratic government has spent the first half of its inaugural five-year term building an orthodox engine for accelerated economic growth. The question now is: Will it start?
Finance Minister Trevor Manuel stated the problem on Friday following the end of the 1996 parliamentary session:

"The economic challenge we face is formidable. Economic growth has been dismal for much of the past 20 years and annual job creation in recent years has not risen above one-third of the net addition to the labour force.
"Income distribution is more unequal than almost anywhere else in the world. Social services face immense backlogs, qualitative deficiencies and organisational fragmentation."

The answer, he said, lay in his June 14 macro-economic framework for growth, employment and redistribution (GEAR), which cemented the swing of the ruling African National Congress (ANC) from its largely socialist liberation agenda to orthodox market eonomics.
The GEAR strategy has displaced President Nelson Mandela's 1994 Reconstruction and Development Programme as the cornerstone of economic policy.

It seeks to harness fiscal discipline, wage and price moderation, industrial incentives and trade liberalisation to encourage local and foreign investment and boost exports, job creation and economic growth by the year 2000.
"The macro-economic strategy argues that these challenges can be confronted and that they must be taken on jointly and simultaneously.
"Growth which does not feed the poor will collapse... redistribution without expanded production cannot be sustained, prosperity without security of life and property holds no appeal," Manuel said.

The government has already bolstered the strategy with tax incentives for new industry and the creation of a new revenue collection agency, a debt management unit and improved monitoring of government spending.
Though the process could take another four years, the government has started to lift exchange controls and the first sales of a promised privatisation programme have taken place.

The state-owned Telkom telecommunications corporation has narrowed the search for a 20 to 30 percent equity partner to four candidates and expects to raise over a billion dollars by the end of March next year.
Manuel has published and repeatedly reaffirmed a timetable to reduce the budget deficit from 5.8 percent of gross domestic product in 1995/96 to three percent by the turn of the century.

Business, industry and International Monetary Fund chief Michel Camdessus have congratulated Manuel on the strategy, but the ANC's allies in government, the Congress of South African Trade Unions (COSATU) and the South African Communist Party, have not.
COSATU and the Communists have criticised the macro-economic strategy as "neo-liberal" and are reviewing their alliance with the ANC heading into the 1999 elections.
Ebrahim Patel, deputy general secretary of the South African Clothing and Textile Workers Union, argued on Friday for a measure of state intervention in the economy.
"The relationship between growth and development is complex ... Economic growth is important, but growth in itself is not an index of human development," he said.
Board of Executors chief economist Rob Lee said Manuel and his team should be congratulated for resisting the pressure from unions and other ANC allies to relax fiscal discipline.
But he said the insistence on gradual reform was allowing South Africa to fall further and further behind its successful developing competitors.
"The markets are giving their verdict. You can see it in the exchange rate," he said in a reference to the rand's 20-percent- plus slide since February.
The rand's decline, which defied central Reserve Bank and government efforts to apply the brakes, has dented foreign reserves and domestic confidence.
Inflation is expected to hit close to 10 percent by the end of 1996 and growth estimates are being revised down to three percent.
